summary: Describes how IPv6 can be deployed in IEEE 802.16 wireless broadband networks next to existing IPv4 services. It covers the main components of IPv6 802.16 access networks, how they differ from IPv4 ones, and how IPv6 is integrated in each 802.16 technology. It is informational.

eli5.summary: This paper is a how-to for adding the newer internet addresses to wireless broadband networks while the older addresses still keep working.

questions: how do you deploy ipv6 in 802.16 networks
what are ipv6 link models in mobile access
subtitle: Deployment strategies for IPv6 in IEEE 802.16 broadband wireless networks.

tldr.problem: IEEE 802.16 (WiMAX) is becoming a major broadband wireless technology, but there is no detailed guidance on how to deploy IPv6 on these networks alongside existing IPv4 services, or how IPv6 addressing, mobility, multicast, and QoS work in wireless 802.16 environments.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5181 provides comprehensive deployment scenarios and architecture guidance for IPv6 in fixed, nomadic, and mobile 802.16 access networks, covering addressing, routing, handover, multicast, security, and network management.
tldr.outcome: Operators can choose appropriate IPv6 deployment models based on whether they are building fixed/nomadic access (like wireless DSL) or mobile access (like mobile WiMAX), and understand the infrastructure changes, protocols, and operational considerations required.

today: RFC 5181 remains Informational and describes deployment scenarios and best practices for IPv6 in IEEE 802.16 networks as they existed in 2008. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: The Challenge of IPv6 in Wireless Broadband
sections.content:
IEEE 802.16 is an air interface standard for fixed and mobile broadband wireless access networks. While the IEEE 802.16 standard defines how to carry IPv4 and IPv6 datagrams over the wireless link, it does not fully specify how IPv6 operates end-to-end in these networks or how to deploy it coexisting with IPv4.

The IEEE 802.16 standards cover only the physical (Layer 1) and medium access control (Layer 2) layers, so they can be used with many different IP network architectures. This document extends earlier IPv6 deployment work to specifically address IEEE 802.16 networks, describing how the main network components differ between IPv4 and IPv6 deployments and how IPv6 is integrated in mobile and fixed access scenarios.
sections.eli5: The 802.16 wireless standard defines how to send packets over the air, but it does not explain in detail how the new internet addresses (IPv6) actually work on these networks or how to set them up. This document gives those missing details.

sections.title: Network Components and Link Models
sections.content:
IEEE 802.16 networks contain several key components: Subscriber Stations (SS) or Mobile Subscriber Stations (MS) are end-user equipment that connect to the network; Base Stations (BS) provide connectivity and control; Access Routers (AR) perform IP routing; and Edge Routers (ER) connect to the Internet Service Provider.

Mobile access scenarios define two possible IPv6 link models. The shared IPv6 prefix link model places all mobile nodes and a single access router interface on one IPv6 subnet, sharing the same prefix. The point-to-point link model allocates a unique prefix or set of prefixes to each MS, treating each MS-to-AR connection as an independent link. Fixed or nomadic access scenarios typically use Ethernet convergence sublayers and resemble wireless DSL deployments, supporting multiple access routers without layer 3 mobility.
sections.eli5: Wireless 802.16 networks have base stations that send the signal, subscriber stations that receive it, and routers that connect to the internet. Depending on whether the users are mobile or stationary, the network assigns addresses differently: either everyone shares one address range, or each user gets their own.

sections.title: IPv6 Addressing and Configuration
sections.content:
In 802.16 networks, an IPv6 mobile subscriber can obtain an IPv6 address in two ways. Stateless auto-configuration uses router discovery and Duplicate Address Detection to allow the MS to automatically configure its address from a prefix the AR announces. DHCPv6 (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6) allows a DHCPv6 server in the service provider core network to assign addresses, with the AR providing relay agent functionality.

In shared prefix models, one or more IPv6 prefixes are assigned to the link and shared by all attached mobile nodes. In point-to-point models, the AR assigns unique prefixes for each MS, and prefix delegation can be used if networks exist behind a mobile subscriber. IPv6 transport typically uses the IPv6 Convergence Sublayer rather than Ethernet Convergence Sublayer to reduce overhead, though Payload Header Suppression mitigates the impact of Ethernet CS overhead.

When the backbone between the AR and ER does not support native IPv6, IPv6-in-IPv4 tunneling can carry IPv6 packets, though native IPv6 is preferred for better scalability and performance.
sections.eli5: Mobile users can get addresses two ways: by asking the network to automatically assign one, or by requesting one from a server like they do in IPv4. Users on the same base station might share one address range, or each might get their own unique range.

sections.title: Mobility, Routing, and Multicast
sections.content:
Handover in 802.16e networks occurs at two levels. A link layer handover happens when a mobile subscriber moves between base stations in the same IPv6 subnet, requiring only a reestablishment of the wireless connection without IP reconfiguration. An IP layer handover occurs when base stations are in different subnets, requiring the MS to acquire new IP configuration. Mobile IPv6 (RFC 3775) handles IP layer handovers, and Fast Handover for Mobile IPv6 (FMIPv6, RFC 4068) can reduce handover latency.

For routing, mobile subscribers typically use a default route pointing to the access router. The access router may support routing protocols like OSPFv3 or IS-IS to multiple edge routers, while the edge router runs the service provider's IGP and redistributes routes to the AR with prefix summarization.

For multicast, IPv6 multicast can be supported via IGMP/MLD proxying and snooping, or potentially through IEEE 802.16 multicast connection identifiers. IPv6 QoS maps to the five 802.16 scheduling services (UGS, rtPS, nrtPS, ertPS, and Best Effort), and management uses SNMP and MIBs that support dual-stack operation.
sections.eli5: When a user moves, the network handles the handover either quickly (if they stay on the same base station) or with an address change (if they move to a different part of the network). Routers forward traffic using standard internet routing protocols. Multicast video or group data is delivered to multiple subscribers, and quality-of-service settings prioritize urgent traffic.

sections.title: Security and Operational Considerations
sections.content:
Authentication occurs at connection initialization when an MS is verified by the AAA (Authentication, Authorization, and Accounting) server at the service provider network. The MS and BS use Privacy Key Management, and the BS communicates with the AAA server using a AAA protocol. Once authenticated, the MS can auto-configure an IPv6 address or obtain one via DHCPv6. This authentication process is the same for IPv4 and IPv6.

The shared prefix link model-based mobile deployments described in RFC 4968 have security implications: protocols designed for private networks may not work safely on public shared-prefix links. This may limit the shared prefix model to enterprise environments where network scope is controlled.

No new security threats are introduced by IPv6 deployment itself; networks should employ the same 802.16e link layer security mechanisms and follow IPv6 transition security considerations defined in RFC 4942.
sections.eli5: When users connect, the network checks their identity with a security server. Then they can use addresses and access the network. Private networks (like in a company) might have stricter rules about who can see whom compared to public broadband networks.
